title: A Linear Model's Out-of-Fold Disagreements Find the Flipped Labels: Filtering Label Noise Without a Clean Set or a Noise Rate
storyline: Symmetric label noise costs a logistic regression many accuracy points, and an untuned MLP trained on the same labels loses far more; the usual fixes need a clean validation set, a noise-rate estimate or deep-network training dynamics. We measure the simplest alternative: predict every training sample with a logistic regression fit on the other folds, drop the samples whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with their given label, and refit on the rest. It works because a sample that models fit without it cannot explain is more likely flipped than one they explain, and the measurement confirms this: in every noisy setting most dropped samples are truly mislabeled and most flipped labels are dropped. The refit model beats plain logistic regression in all but one paired noisy run and the untuned MLP in every one, recovering most of the lost accuracy in three of four noisy settings, while on clean labels it costs a fraction of a point and the MLP ties or wins. Before reaching for a bigger model or a noise-rate estimate, a linear model's own out-of-fold errors already clean most symmetric noise on small problems; we make no claim beyond two small datasets and symmetric flips.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.goal: The reader knows the gap (noise cleaning usually needs a clean set, a noise rate or a deep model), the one-line rule, why it works, what the small study shows, and its scope.
points: One paragraph. Open with the flaw of current practice: methods that clean noisy labels need a clean validation set, a noise-rate estimate or a deep network, and it is unclear how far a plain linear model gets without any of them.

State the rule in one sentence: fit logistic regression with K-fold cross-validation on the noisy labels, drop every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label, and refit on the rest; it uses no clean data and no noise rate.
One sentence on why it works: a sample that models fit on other folds cannot explain is more likely mislabeled than one they explain.

Evidence in general terms: on two small datasets with symmetric noise up to 40% (noise_high_pct), most dropped samples are truly flipped (pooled precision about 71%, precision_pooled_noisy) and most flipped labels are dropped; the refit model beats plain logistic regression in all but one paired noisy run and an untuned MLP trained on the same labels in every one. Do not print the run denominators.

Cost and scope: on clean labels the filter costs a fraction of a point and the MLP ties or slightly wins; this is a small study and makes no claim about deep networks, large data or other noise types. Code availability sentence (no URL in review mode; say code is released).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.goal: The reader believes that a linear model's out-of-fold disagreements are mostly the flipped labels, that dropping them and refitting is a simple, checkable alternative to methods needing a clean set or noise rate, and knows exactly what this small study does and does not show.
points: Problem (practitioner view): training labels contain flips, and a logistic regression trained on them loses many accuracy points, more as the noise rate grows; a more flexible model trained on the same labels loses far more (say 'in our runs, an untuned MLP falls further', as an observation, not a mechanism). One sentence on why labels get flipped, no AI-importance opener.

Gap: current cleaning methods need something the practitioner often lacks: a clean validation set, an estimate of the noise rate or transition matrix (loss correction), or the training dynamics of deep networks (small-loss selection, co-teaching). Cite the Song et al. survey, co-teaching and loss correction. Confident learning also uses out-of-sample predictions, but adds per-class thresholds and noise-count estimation; cross-validated filters go back to Brodley and Friedl. What is missing is a plain, checkable measurement of how far the simplest version takes a linear model.

Idea and reason, with Figure 1 referenced here: predict each training sample with a logistic regression fit on the other folds, drop the samples it disagrees with, refit. State the central claim once in italics: *a linear model's out-of-fold disagreements are mostly the flipped labels*. One sentence on why: under symmetric noise a flipped label conflicts with the class structure the other folds learn, so the out-of-fold model predicts against it far more often than against a clean label. The rule takes no noise rate and no clean data.

Evidence first, in words: in every noisy setting most dropped samples are truly mislabeled (pooled precision about 71%, precision_pooled_noisy) and most flipped labels are dropped; the refit model beats plain logistic regression in all but one paired noisy run and the untuned MLP in every one, across symmetric noise up to 40% (noise_high_pct). On clean labels it costs a fraction of a point. Do not print run denominators.

Lead-in sentence, then three contributions as a bulleted list, each a bold lead-in and one verb-first sentence: (1) \textbf{Out-of-fold disagreement finds flipped labels.} We show that the samples a cross-validated logistic regression disagrees with are mostly truly mislabeled, and that most flipped labels are among them, in every noisy setting we ran. (2) \textbf{A filter with no clean set and no noise rate.} We present the drop-and-refit filter and show that it beats plain logistic regression and an untuned MLP trained on the same noisy labels under symmetric noise. (3) \textbf{An honest account of cost and scope.} We report where it does not help: a small clean-label cost, a tie with the MLP on clean data, an unstable high-noise cell, about five times the fit time, and a scope of two small datasets and symmetric noise.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.goal: The reader sees where the filter sits: it is the oldest, simplest form of cross-validated filtering, measured carefully for a linear model, and it is not compared against deep sample-selection methods or confident learning.
points: \paragraph{Learning with noisy labels.} The surveys (Song et al. for deep networks, Frenay and Verleysen for classical classifiers) group methods into loss correction with a transition matrix (Patrini et al.), noise-tolerant losses (Ghosh et al.), noise models built into logistic regression (Bootkrajang and Kaban; Lee and Jung) and sample selection. Close with: our filter changes neither the loss nor the model and needs no noise model.

\paragraph{Sample selection in deep networks.} Co-teaching exchanges small-loss samples between two networks, Co-teaching+ selects among samples where the two networks disagree, and Area Under the Margin ranks samples by training dynamics. Close with: these rely on deep-network training dynamics; we use the out-of-fold prediction of a linear model and do not compare against them.

\paragraph{Cross-validated filtering and confident learning.} Brodley and Friedl remove training instances misclassified by models trained on other folds (single-algorithm, majority and consensus filters); confident learning prunes using out-of-sample predicted probabilities with per-class thresholds and noise-count estimates. Close with: our rule is the single-algorithm filter with logistic regression and a plain argmax disagreement; what we add is a checkable measurement of its precision, recall, accuracy gain and clean-label cost, not a new filtering idea. State only what the related-work notes verify; no numbers in this section.

sections.title: Out-of-Fold Disagreement Filter
sections.goal: The reader can implement the filter from this section alone and sees why disagreement with an out-of-fold prediction should mark a flipped label.
points: Notation, defined once: training set D = {(x_i, \tilde{y}_i)}_{i=1}^n with observed, possibly flipped labels \tilde{y}_i; a classifier f (standardized logistic regression) maps x to a predicted class. Describe the filter as a function: it takes D and returns a model trained on a subset S of D.

Step 1, in words then one equation: split D into K stratified folds; for sample i in fold k(i), the out-of-fold prediction \hat{y}_i is the class predicted by f fit on all folds except k(i). Step 2: keep S = {i : \hat{y}_i = \tilde{y}_i}, dropping every sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its label. Step 3: refit f on S with the given labels. We use K = 5 (filter_folds). The rule has no threshold, uses no noise rate and holds out no clean data; it costs K + 1 fits.

Why it should work, one short paragraph stated as an argument (not a guarantee): under symmetric noise a flipped label is inconsistent with the class structure learned from the other folds, so the out-of-fold model tends to predict the true class and the sample is dropped, while a clean sample is kept whenever that model is right. The price is that clean samples the model gets wrong are dropped too; Section 5 measures both how often the dropped samples are truly flipped and what the clean-label drops cost. One sentence relating it to the cross-validated filter of Brodley and Friedl, which this rule instantiates with logistic regression.

sections.title: Experimental Setup
sections.goal: A reviewer can check the data, noise model, baselines, metrics and statistics in one compact read, and sees the study's scope stated plainly.
points: \paragraph{Data and noise.} Two scikit-learn datasets: digits (10 classes) and breast cancer (2 classes), with n_train_digits and n_train_breast_cancer training samples after a stratified split. Symmetric noise flips each training label with probability 20% or 40% (noise_low_pct, noise_high_pct) to a class drawn uniformly from the others; 0% is the clean reference. Test labels are never corrupted.

\paragraph{Models.} Plain logistic regression with C = logreg_C on standardized features, trained on the noisy labels; an MLP with one hidden layer of mlp_hidden units and at most mlp_max_iter iterations, scikit-learn defaults otherwise and untuned; and the filter with filter_folds folds wrapping the same logistic regression. We run no other noise-robust method (co-teaching, confident learning), no clean-label oracle and no ablation over folds, C or MLP size.

\paragraph{Metrics and statistics.} Accuracy on the clean test split (test_fraction_pct% of each dataset). For the filter: precision (share of dropped samples that were truly flipped), recall (share of flipped samples dropped) and recovered share, (filter - logreg) / (logreg at 0% - logreg), our own definition. Each setting is run with n_seeds seeds; a seed fixes the split, the noise draw, the folds and the MLP initialization, and all methods share them, so comparisons are paired. Paired two-sided t-tests over seeds; precision tested against 50% with a one-sample t-test. Realized noise at nominal 40% is slightly lower (noisy_pct_digits_n40, noisy_pct_breast_cancer_n40); mention only if space allows, otherwise drop and keep to four numbers in this paragraph.

sections.title: Results
sections.goal: The reader sees four findings, each opened by its verdict and backed by a table or figure: disagreements are mostly flipped labels, filtering beats plain logistic regression (more at higher noise on digits, with one unstable cell), it beats an untuned MLP on noisy labels, and on clean labels it costs little while the MLP ties or wins.
points: Lead paragraph (two sentences, no numbers): out-of-fold disagreement finds most flipped labels, and the refit model gains accuracy under noise at little cost on clean labels; Table 1 holds accuracies, Table 2 the drop statistics, Figure 2 the paired gains.

Subsection 'The filter drops mostly flipped labels and finds most of them': verdict first; mean precision is above 50% in all four noisy cells and every test against 50% is significant (Table 2); pooled precision about 71% (precision_pooled_noisy), and even the worst seed in the hardest cell stays above half (precision_min_breast_cancer_n40). Recall is high, highest on digits where nearly every flipped label is dropped (Table 2). Note that a quarter to a third of dropped samples are clean.

Subsection 'Filtering beats plain logistic regression, more so at higher noise', paragraph 1: noise costs logistic regression many points and the cost grows with the noise rate on both datasets (Table 1); the filter wins on digits at both noise rates, and the gain grows from 20% to 40% noise (digits gain at 40%, diff_filter_logreg_digits_n40; trend test p_trend_dg_gain_lr), see Figure 2.

Same subsection, paragraph 2: on breast cancer the filter wins clearly at 40% noise, while at 20% the gain is positive on average but not significant with five seeds (p_bc20_filter_vs_lr), and the rise of the gain with noise is not significant there (p_trend_bc_gain_lr). State these as limits, not hedges.

Same subsection, paragraph 3: the filter regains most of the accuracy noise costs logistic regression in three of four noisy cells (Table 2, recovered column), but only about a fifth on breast cancer at 40% noise (recovered_breast_cancer_n40), where both the filter and logistic regression vary by about 9 points across seeds (sd_filter_breast_cancer_n40); we put no tight claim on that cell.

Subsection 'A filtered linear model beats an untuned MLP on the same noisy labels': verdict first; the filter beats the MLP in every paired noisy run, with gaps from about 11 points (diff_filter_mlp_breast_cancer_n20) to about 28 points (diff_filter_mlp_digits_n40) that grow with noise (Table 1, Figure 2). The MLP falls to about 65% at 40% noise on both datasets, far below logistic regression; this is consistent with a flexible model fitting the wrong labels (cite memorization work), but we did not test that explanation, and the MLP was not tuned or early-stopped.

Subsection 'With clean labels the filter costs little and the MLP ties or wins', paragraph 1: at 0% noise the filter loses at most a fraction of a point to logistic regression (cost_clean_digits), not significant (Table 1), because it still discards a few correctly labeled samples (about 3.5% of digits, dropped_pct_digits_n0; give breast cancer, dropped_pct_breast_cancer_n0, in a separate sentence or paragraph so no paragraph exceeds two numbers).

Same subsection, paragraph 2: on clean labels the untuned MLP is as good as or slightly better than the filter: under one point in its favor on digits (diff_filter_mlp_digits_n0) and no significant gap on breast cancer. The filter also takes about five times the fit time of logistic regression on digits (time_filter_over_logreg_digits_n0, indicative, machine unknown), from the K cross-validation fits and the refit.

sections.title: Discussion and Limitations
sections.goal: The reader leaves with the big picture (check a linear model's own out-of-fold errors before reaching for a bigger model or a noise-rate estimate) and a short, plain list of what the study does not show, framed as next steps.
points: What it changes: the simplest cross-validated filter, applied to a linear model, already finds most symmetric flips and turns them into accuracy, with no clean data and no noise rate. For practitioners with small tabular-scale problems, this is the first thing to try and a baseline any noise-robust method should beat; the flexible model is the one that suffered most from noise in our runs. Keep the scope words 'small problems' and 'symmetric noise'.

Limitations as future work, one paragraph: two small datasets, five seeds, one noise type (symmetric flips); no comparison with co-teaching or confident learning; no ablation over folds, C or MLP size; the MLP was untuned, so the gap is against an untuned MLP; breast cancer at 40% noise is unstable across seeds; five seeds cannot prove the clean-label cost is zero; the filter takes about five times the fit time. Next steps: class-dependent and instance-dependent noise, a tuned or early-stopped MLP, comparison with confident learning on the same splits. No claim about deep networks or large data.
Closing sentence (optional): the dropped set is itself an output, a short list of suspect labels a person can review.

figures.message: A logistic regression's out-of-fold disagreements are mostly the flipped labels, so dropping them and refitting keeps accuracy near the clean level while plain logistic regression and an untuned MLP fall with noise.
figures.spec: Three flat pastel panels left to right with rounded corners, numbered circles and plain sans-serif titles. Panel 1 (circle 1, 'Noisy labels'): a small grid of training samples (digit-like thumbnails or dots) with class tags; a few tags flipped and marked in a red outline. Panel 2 (circle 2, 'Out-of-fold check'): five fold blocks; one highlighted fold is predicted by a network-card icon fit on the other four (purple #4E2A84); samples whose prediction disagrees with their tag are crossed out. Below it a single horizontal stacked bar of all dropped samples pooled over the noisy runs, split into 'truly flipped' (purple) and 'clean' (lavender #F1EEF7 with purple outline), labeled with pooled precision (precision_pooled_noisy). Panel 3 (circle 3, 'Refit'): grouped bar chart drawn from results/runs.jsonl, two small groups (Digits, Breast cancer), x = noise 0/20/40%, bars for Logistic regression (muted blue), MLP (muted orange) and Filter (#4E2A84), mean over 5 seeds, sd error bars, individual seed points; y axis 'Test accuracy (%)' from 50 to 100. A thick rounded arrow links each panel to the next. Labels one to three words; no equations. Use the same baseline hues in Figure 2.
figures.caption: Out-of-fold disagreement finds flipped labels, and refitting without them keeps a linear model accurate under label noise. (1) A training set with symmetric label flips. (2) Each sample is predicted by a logistic regression fit on the other folds; samples whose prediction disagrees with their label are dropped, and most of the dropped samples are truly flipped (bar, pooled over all noisy runs). (3) Test accuracy of plain logistic regression, an untuned MLP and the refit filter at 0, 20 and 40% noise; bars are means over all 5 seeds (not selected cases), error bars are sd, and dots are seeds. The filter stays closest to its clean-label accuracy as noise grows, while the MLP falls furthest.

figures.message: The filter's paired gain over both baselines is near zero or slightly negative on clean labels and grows with the noise rate, clearly so on digits.
figures.spec: Two side-by-side small panels sharing a y axis: Digits (left), Breast cancer (right). x: noise rate 0%, 20%, 40%. Grouped bars: per-seed paired accuracy difference filter minus logistic regression (muted blue, same hue as logistic regression in Figure 1) and filter minus MLP (muted orange, same hue as MLP), mean over 5 seeds, sd error bars, individual seed points overlaid in a darker shade. Horizontal zero line in gray. y axis 'Accuracy gain of filter (points)', about -3 to 33. Legend above the panels, off the data. No titles inside the plot; panel names as small labels.
figures.caption: The filter's accuracy gain grows with label noise. Bars show the paired test-accuracy difference between the filter and each baseline (logistic regression, untuned MLP) at each noise rate; bars are means over 5 seeds, error bars are sd, and dots are individual seeds. Values below zero mean the baseline is better. On clean labels the gain is near zero against logistic regression and slightly negative against the MLP on digits; under noise every seed favors the filter over the MLP, and on digits the gain over logistic regression grows from 20 to 40% noise.
